questions.question: What is Spring Boot and why was it created?
questions.title: What is Spring Boot?
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot is an opinionated framework built on top of Spring that eliminates boilerplate configuration. It was created to solve the problem that vanilla Spring required hundreds of lines of XML or Java configuration just to start a project. Spring Boot uses convention-over-configuration — sensible defaults get you running, and you override only what you need.
questions.interviewer_intent: Almost every Java interview starts here. Test whether the candidate understands Spring Boot's core value proposition.

sections.content: Spring Boot was born out of frustration with how much setup Spring required. To build a simple REST API with classic Spring you'd need to configure a DispatcherServlet, set up component scanning, configure a ViewResolver, wire up Jackson, deploy to a Tomcat separately — pages of configuration before writing a single line of business logic. Spring Boot collapses all of that. You add the right starter dependency, annotate your class, and run it. The embedded server, the JSON converter, the component scan — all configured automatically based on what's on your classpath. That's the core promise: convention over configuration.
Spring Boot = Spring + sensible defaults + embedded server + starter dependencies. Convention over configuration.

speakable_v2.hook: Before Spring Boot, starting a REST API meant pages of XML config before writing a single business line.

beats.text: Spring Boot is an opinionated layer on top of Spring. It bundles sensible defaults so you don't have to configure everything from scratch. Think of it this way: classic Spring hands you all the parts; Spring Boot hands you an assembled engine. The standard example is a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application — you annotate one class, add a starter dependency, and you're serving HTTP responses. Zero XML.

The core idea is convention over configuration. Spring Boot assumes reasonable defaults for the embedded server, JSON serialization, and component scanning. You only override what you actually need to change. That's why teams can go from zero to a running API in minutes instead of hours.

seo.meta_description: Understand what Spring Boot is, why it was created, and its core value proposition of convention over configuration.

questions.question: What does @SpringBootApplication do?
questions.title: @SpringBootApplication annotation explained
questions.direct_answer: @SpringBootApplication is a convenience annotation that combines three annotations: @Configuration (marks the class as a config source), @EnableAutoConfiguration (triggers Spring Boot's auto-configuration), and @ComponentScan (scans the current package and sub-packages for Spring components).
questions.interviewer_intent: Test knowledge of the core annotation — a common first follow-up after 'what is Spring Boot'.

sections.content: It's a meta-annotation — it wraps three separate annotations so you don't have to write all three. @Configuration tells Spring this class can define beans. @EnableAutoConfiguration is the key one — it tells Spring Boot to look at your classpath and automatically configure things. If it sees spring-web on the classpath, it sets up a web server. If it sees JPA, it sets up a datasource. @ComponentScan makes Spring look for @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller annotations in the same package and below. Together these three do all the foundational setup.

rows: Marks class as a bean definition source
Scans package for @Component and related annotations

speakable_v2.hook: That one annotation on your main class is actually doing three jobs at once.

beats.text: SpringBootApplication is a shortcut — a meta-annotation that combines three separate annotations. Instead of remembering to add all three every time, you write one and get all three. Here's what each one does.

rows: Tells Spring this class can define beans
Scans your classpath and auto-wires matching config

beats.text: The most powerful of the three is @EnableAutoConfiguration. That's the one that sees spring-web on your classpath and quietly sets up Tomcat and Jackson for you. The other two are housekeeping — but all three are needed for a working app.

followup_questions: What is the base package for @ComponentScan?

seo.meta_description: Understand what @SpringBootApplication does — it combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan.

questions.question: What happens when you run SpringApplication.run()?
questions.title: Spring Boot application startup sequence
questions.direct_answer: SpringApplication.run() bootstraps the application: creates the ApplicationContext, triggers auto-configuration, starts the embedded web server (if web is on the classpath), performs component scanning to find beans, wires dependencies, and runs any CommandLineRunner or ApplicationRunner beans. The app is ready to serve requests after this returns.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests understanding of what happens under the hood — distinguishes candidates who understand Spring from those who just use it.

sections.content: When run() is called, several things happen in order. First, Spring Boot figures out what type of ApplicationContext to create — a web context if web is on the classpath, a reactive context for WebFlux, or a plain context otherwise. Then it runs auto-configuration: scans the classpath and applies configuration classes. Then component scanning finds all your @Service, @Repository, @Controller classes. Then dependency injection wires everything together. Then the embedded Tomcat (or Jetty, Netty) starts and begins listening on the configured port. Finally, any CommandLineRunner beans execute. The whole process takes a second or two.
Startup sequence: create context → auto-configure → component scan → wire beans → start server → run runners.

speakable_v2.hook: That one line of code in main triggers a six-step chain before your app is ready to take requests.

beats.text: SpringApplication.run does a lot. It's not just 'start the server.' Here's the order things happen in a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application.

items: Create the ApplicationContext — Spring Boot picks the right type based on your classpath (web, reactive, or plain).
Run auto-configuration — it reads your classpath and applies matching config classes automatically.
Component scan — finds all your @Service, @Repository, and @Controller classes in the same package.
Wire dependencies — injects beans everywhere they're needed.
Start the embedded server — Tomcat listens on port 8080 by default.
Run CommandLineRunner beans — any startup logic you've registered executes last.

beats.text: The whole sequence takes a second or two. After run() returns, your app is live. That's why understanding this order helps when you're debugging slow startup or missing beans.

followup_questions: What is the difference between CommandLineRunner and ApplicationRunner?

seo.meta_description: Understand what happens when SpringApplication.run() is called — the Spring Boot startup sequence explained.

questions.question: What is the Spring Boot parent POM and why do projects use it?
questions.title: Spring Boot parent POM and dependency management
questions.direct_answer: The Spring Boot parent POM (spring-boot-starter-parent) provides dependency management — it defines versions for hundreds of commonly used libraries that are known to work together. By inheriting from it, you don't need to specify versions for most Spring and third-party dependencies. It also configures sensible Maven plugin defaults.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests project setup knowledge — understanding that the parent POM solves dependency version conflicts.

sections.content: One of the most painful parts of pre-Boot Spring projects was managing library versions. If you chose Jackson 2.14 and Spring 5.3, you had to know they were compatible. Miss a version mismatch and you'd get runtime errors. The parent POM solves this by pre-testing a set of library versions that work together. It's a bill-of-materials approach. You declare spring-boot-starter-parent as your parent, and then when you add dependencies you can often omit the version — the parent POM supplies a tested version. This is why you see so many Spring Boot pom.xml files with version-less dependency entries.

<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>3.2.0</version>
</parent>
<dependencies>
  <!-- No version needed — parent manages it -->
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
Parent POM = tested dependency versions + plugin defaults. You get version-conflict-free builds without specifying individual versions.

speakable_v2.hook: Version mismatches used to crash Spring projects at runtime. The parent POM was created to fix exactly that.

beats.text: Before the parent POM, you had to manually pick compatible versions of Spring, Jackson, Hibernate, and every other library. Get one wrong and you'd see cryptic runtime errors. The spring-boot-starter-parent solves this with a bill-of-materials approach — the Spring team pre-tests a set of library versions that work together and publishes that list as the parent POM.

In practice this means you declare the parent POM once with its version, and then you can add dependencies like spring-boot-starter-web without specifying a version number. The parent supplies a tested, compatible version automatically. It also sets up sensible Maven plugin defaults, so your builds behave consistently without extra config.

followup_questions: What if you can't use the parent POM (multi-module project)?

seo.meta_title: Spring Boot Parent POM Explained | InterviewExplainer
seo.meta_description: Understand the Spring Boot parent POM and how it provides dependency management for Spring projects.

questions.question: What is the Spring Initializr and how do you use it?
questions.title: Spring Initializr — project bootstrapping
questions.direct_answer: Spring Initializr (start.spring.io) is a web tool to generate a Spring Boot project structure. You select the build tool (Maven/Gradle), Spring Boot version, Java version, and dependencies, then download a ZIP with the correct pom.xml, directory structure, and a starter main class. It eliminates manual project setup.
questions.interviewer_intent: Practical question about project setup — shows the candidate has actually used Spring Boot.

sections.content: Spring Initializr is the starting point for any new Spring Boot project. You go to start.spring.io, choose Maven or Gradle, pick your Java version, enter your group and artifact IDs, and then — the important part — search for and add the dependencies you need: Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, Spring Security, whatever fits your project. Hit Generate, download the ZIP, extract it, open in your IDE. The pom.xml is already correct, the directory structure is set up, and there's a main class ready to run. Most IDEs like IntelliJ and Eclipse also have Initializr built in so you don't even need the browser.
start.spring.io generates a ready-to-run project. Also available inside IntelliJ IDEA (File > New > Spring Initializr).

speakable_v2.hook: Every Spring Boot project starts somewhere — and that somewhere is usually start.spring.io.

beats.text: Spring Initializr is a code generator for new projects. You make a few choices on the website, hit Generate, and get a ZIP with a fully wired project ready to open. Here's the flow.

items: Go to start.spring.io and pick Maven or Gradle as your build tool.
Select your Java version and Spring Boot version (e.g., 3.2).
Enter group and artifact IDs — these become your package name and JAR name.
Search for and add dependencies: Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, whatever you need.
Hit Generate, download the ZIP, extract it, and open in IntelliJ or Eclipse.

beats.text: IntelliJ IDEA also has Initializr built in under File > New > Spring Initializr, so you don't even need the browser. Either way, you skip all the manual pom.xml wiring and start writing actual code right away.

followup_questions: What is the difference between Maven and Gradle in this context?
Can you use Spring Boot without Spring Initializr?

seo.meta_description: Learn how to use Spring Initializr to bootstrap a Spring Boot project quickly.

questions.question: What is the difference between a fat JAR and a regular JAR in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Spring Boot fat JAR (uber JAR)
questions.direct_answer: A fat JAR (or uber JAR) includes the application code and all dependencies in a single JAR file. Regular JARs only contain the application code — dependencies must be on the classpath separately. Spring Boot's Maven/Gradle plugins produce a fat JAR by default, so you can run the app with a single java -jar command.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests deployment knowledge — understanding the packaging model is important for DevOps-aware candidates.

sections.content: In a traditional Java project, when you build a JAR it only contains your code. To run it you'd need to have all the library JARs on the classpath, which means managing a lib folder or deploying to an application server. Spring Boot's build plugins repackage your JAR into a fat JAR — it contains your code plus all the dependency JARs packed inside. The embedded Tomcat is in there too. So you can take that one JAR file, put it on any machine with Java installed, run java -jar myapp.jar, and it starts up. That's what makes Docker-based deployments so clean with Spring Boot.

# Build fat JAR
./mvnw package
# Run it — no classpath needed
java -jar target/myapp-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
Fat JAR = self-contained executable. One file, one command, no external dependencies needed at runtime.

speakable_v2.hook: A regular JAR is just your code. A Spring Boot fat JAR is your code plus everything it needs to run — in one file.

beats.text: The difference comes down to what's inside the JAR file and what that means for deployment.

rows: Your code + all dependencies + embedded Tomcat

beats.text: Spring Boot's Maven and Gradle plugins produce a fat JAR automatically when you run the package command. That's why a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application deploys so cleanly to Docker — you just copy one file and run it. No lib folder, no Tomcat installation, no classpath setup.

followup_questions: What is the BOOT-INF directory inside a Spring Boot JAR?

seo.meta_title: Spring Boot Fat JAR Uber JAR Explained | InterviewExplainer
seo.meta_description: Understand what a Spring Boot fat JAR is and why it simplifies deployment to a single java -jar command.

questions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator?
questions.title: Spring Boot Actuator for production monitoring
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot Actuator adds production-ready monitoring endpoints to your application. Add the spring-boot-starter-actuator dependency and you get HTTP endpoints like /actuator/health (is the app up?), /actuator/info (app metadata), /actuator/metrics (JVM stats, request counts), and more — all with no extra code.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests awareness of production concerns — shows the candidate thinks beyond just writing code.

sections.content: Actuator is a production monitoring add-on. In a real deployment you need to know: is my application healthy, how much memory is it using, how many requests per second is it handling. Actuator provides this through HTTP endpoints or JMX beans. The most important one is /actuator/health — load balancers use this to know if the instance is ready to receive traffic. /actuator/metrics exposes JVM metrics, HTTP request counts, database connection pool stats. You can integrate this with monitoring tools like Prometheus and Grafana. It's a one-dependency addition that gives you significant observability.
/actuator/health is the liveness/readiness check used by Kubernetes and load balancers. Enabled by default.

speakable_v2.hook: Once your app is deployed, you need to know it's healthy. Actuator gives you that visibility with one dependency.

beats.text: Spring Boot Actuator is a monitoring add-on. Add the spring-boot-starter-actuator dependency and your app immediately exposes a set of HTTP endpoints that answer operational questions. No extra code needed.

items: /actuator/health — tells load balancers and Kubernetes whether your app is up and ready.
/actuator/info — returns metadata like app version and description.
/actuator/metrics — exposes JVM memory, request counts, and database pool stats.
These integrate directly with monitoring tools like Prometheus and Grafana.

beats.text: The health endpoint is the most critical one in production. Kubernetes uses it to decide whether to route traffic to your pod. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, /actuator/health is enabled by default and requires zero configuration to start using.

followup_questions: How do you secure Actuator endpoints?
How do you expose custom health indicators?

seo.meta_description: Learn what Spring Boot Actuator is and how it adds health checks and monitoring endpoints to your application.
